opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of the LEACE paper, which stands for LEAst-squares Concept Erasure. The starting point is a question: what does it actually mean for a representation to not contain a concept, at least from the perspective of linear models?

We formalized that as linear guardedness. A representation is linearly guarded with respect to some concept if no linear classifier can predict that concept better than a trivial constant predictor that ignores the input. The nice thing we were able to show is that this has a very clean equivalent characterization. For a broad class of loss functions, basically any convex loss like cross-entropy or squared error, linear guardedness holds exactly when the class-conditional means of the representation are all equal. Equivalently, the cross-covariance between the representation X and the one-hot encoded concept label Z is zero. So this fuzzy, behavioral notion of "no linear classifier can do better than chance" collapses into a single algebraic condition: make that cross-covariance matrix vanish.

Once you have that, the second half of the question becomes a well-posed optimization problem. There are infinitely many ways to zero out the cross-covariance. You could just map everything to zero, which is useless. What we actually want is to destroy the concept while preserving everything else as much as possible. So we ask: among all affine transformations of X that achieve zero cross-covariance with Z, which one minimizes the expected squared distance between the original and the edited representation? That's the least-squares part.

It turns out this has a closed-form solution. Roughly, you whiten the data so the covariance is the identity. In that whitened space you project out the subspace spanned by the cross-covariance with the concept, the directions that carry the linearly available information about Z. Then you un-whiten back to the original space. The overall map is an oblique projection rather than a plain orthogonal one, and that's important. If you just orthogonally project out the difference-in-means direction in the raw coordinates, you can leave residual correlations behind because the features are correlated with each other. The whitening accounts for that.

So the conceptual link is this. Linear guardedness tells you exactly what constraint you need to satisfy, which is zero cross-covariance. The minimal-change criterion picks out the unique best transformation satisfying that constraint. And because it's provably the minimal edit, you get a principled guarantee: you've removed exactly the linearly decodable information about the concept, and anything else you changed was necessary to do that. That's what makes it useful for things like fairness interventions or causal probing, where you want to argue that a downstream change in behavior came from removing the concept and not from collateral damage to the representation.

The main caveat is that this is all linear. A nonlinear probe might still recover the concept, and we've done follow-up work on quadratic and higher-order erasure. But for the linear case, there's a nice tight story where the definition and the optimal method fit together almost perfectly.

r001.rationale: It states that linear guardedness holds exactly when class-conditional representation means are all equal; for a binary concept, that means the two classes have equal means.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing the affine transformation that minimizes expected squared distance from the original representation, subject to zero cross-covariance with the concept, which it identifies as the linear guardedness condition.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that linear guardedness is really a constraint, and "change the representation as little as possible" is an objective, and LEACE is what you get when you put those two together and actually solve the optimization problem in closed form.

Let me unpack that a bit. Linear guardedness, in the sense that Ravfogel and others defined it, says that no linear classifier can do better than chance at predicting the concept from the representation. And there's a nice equivalence we proved: a representation is linearly guarded with respect to a concept if and only if every class-conditional mean is the same. So if you take the mean embedding of all the examples labeled "male" and the mean embedding of all the examples labeled "female," those have to coincide. Equivalently, the cross-covariance between the representation and the one-hot label vector has to be zero. That's the entire content of the condition. It's actually quite a weak condition — it says nothing about higher-order statistics, nothing about what a nonlinear probe could do. It's just the first moment.

Now, once you know that, the question becomes: what's the smallest edit I can make to the representation that forces those class means to line up? And "smallest" we measure in mean squared error, so we want the affine map that minimizes the expected squared distance between the original embedding and the edited embedding, subject to the constraint that the cross-covariance with the labels is zero.

And it turns out this has a clean closed-form solution. You end up projecting out a subspace, but — and this is the important part — you don't project out in the standard Euclidean metric. You whiten the representation first, using the covariance of the data, do an orthogonal projection in that whitened space onto the orthogonal complement of the span of the class-mean differences, and then unwhiten. So it's an oblique projection in the original coordinates. The reason it's oblique is that the covariance of the representation tells you which directions are "cheap" to move in and which are "expensive," and the least-squares-optimal solution exploits that structure.

The intuition I'd give is this: if you did a naive orthogonal projection, like just removing the direction between the two class means, you'd be throwing away information that's correlated with the concept but isn't actually necessary to remove in order to achieve guardedness. The whitening step accounts for the fact that the concept direction is entangled with other directions through the covariance, and the optimal surgery removes only the part that's actually needed to make the means coincide. In a lot of cases that's a lower-dimensional, more surgical change than what people were doing with things like iterative nullspace projection, which would often take many iterations and chew up a lot of the signal.

So to directly answer the question: the mathematical connection is that linear guardedness reduces to a linear equality constraint on the first moment of the representation, and minimizing the change you make, measured in a quadratic norm, subject to a linear equality constraint, is a standard constrained least-squares problem. That's why there's a closed form at all. And the geometry of that closed form is "project orthogonally in the whitened metric," which is just what minimum-norm solutions to linear constraints always look like once you account for the right inner product.

One thing I'd add is that this framing also makes clear what the method doesn't do. It guarantees nothing against nonlinear probes, because nonlinear probes can use second-order and higher statistics that the constraint leaves untouched. We were pretty upfront about that. The guarantee is exactly as strong as the constraint, no stronger. But within the linear regime, it's provably the least-destructive thing you can do, and empirically that shows up as much smaller damage to the model's downstream behavior than earlier erasure methods.

r001.rationale: It states that linear guardedness holds iff every class-conditional mean is the same, including the two binary concept classes.

r002.rationale: It describes finding the affine map that minimizes expected squared distance from the original representation, subject to the constraint that makes it linearly guarded.

astra-6.text:
The connection is that you can formulate linear guardedness as a constraint, and then ask for the smallest change to the representation that satisfies that constraint.

Suppose X is your representation and Z is the concept you want to erase. In the setting we’re considering, linear guardedness amounts to making the cross-covariance between X and Z zero. For a categorical concept, represented with one-hot labels, that means the class-conditional means are all the same. So a linear predictor can’t exploit differences between those means to improve on a constant prediction.

Then you look for an affine transformation of X that satisfies that condition while minimizing the expected squared distance between the original representation and the transformed representation. That’s the least-squares concept erasure problem.

Geometrically, you can understand the solution by whitening the representation, projecting out the directions that carry cross-covariance with the concept, and then undoing the whitening. In the original coordinates, that’s generally an oblique projection rather than an orthogonal one. The covariance structure matters for figuring out what you actually need to change.

So guardedness specifies what information a linear predictor should no longer be able to use, and the minimum-change objective picks the transformation that accomplishes that with the least distortion. It doesn’t imply that a nonlinear predictor can’t recover the concept.

r001.rationale: It says linear guardedness requires zero cross-covariance and explains that, for categorical concepts, this means all class-conditional means are equal. This covers equal means for the two classes of a binary concept.

r002.rationale: It describes finding an affine transformation that achieves guardedness while minimizing expected squared distance from the original representation.

sol-6.1.text:
The connection is that you can treat linear guardedness as a constraint, and then ask for the smallest change to the representation that satisfies that constraint.

Roughly, guardedness means that a linear predictor can’t use the representation to predict some concept better than it could just by knowing the concept’s average. In the least-squares setting, that amounts to making the cross-covariance between the representation and the concept zero.

But there are lots of ways to do that. You could throw away the whole representation, and that would certainly remove the information. So we add an objective: minimize the expected squared distance between the original representation and the edited one. That gives you a precise sense in which you’re removing the linearly predictive information while preserving as much else as possible.

The subtlety is that simply projecting orthogonally away from the concept directions generally isn’t the least-change solution, because the representation’s coordinates are correlated and have different variances. You have to account for that covariance structure. That’s what gives you the LEACE construction: you can understand it through whitening, projecting out the relevant directions, and transforming back. In the original coordinates, the resulting map is generally an oblique projection.

r001.rationale: It describes guardedness via zero cross-covariance with a concept, but does not state the binary-concept equivalence to equal mean representations across the two classes.

r002.rationale: It says to minimize expected squared distance from the original representation while imposing guardedness, which captures the least-squares surgical transformation.
